hook.title: The chatbot that apologised 400 times
hook.why: It's your first Monday at Orbit Outdoor. Over the weekend, hundreds of customers asked the website chatbot where their order was. It answered every one of them instantly and politely, and helped none of them.
hook.narration: It's nine in the morning on Monday, your first week at Orbit Outdoor. Over the weekend, four hundred customers asked the website chatbot where their order was. The chatbot answered every single one, instantly and politely. And every answer was the same: sorry, I can't access order information. Now Leo's queue is full of angry follow-ups, and Maya wants to know what went wrong. Before anyone explains anything: what do you think the chatbot was missing?

messages.text: morning. weekend queue: 400 new tickets. i've opened 40 so far and every single one is some version of "where is my order"
and the bot answered all of them. same reply every time: "I'm sorry, I can't access order information." now they're writing back. angrier.
we pay for that bot every month. it can write a poem about tents but it can't tell ana where hers is?
you've got fresh eyes. before priya and i decide anything: what is it actually missing?

hook.prompt: Before anything is explained: why couldn't the chatbot answer a single order question?

hunches.label: It needs a bigger, smarter model that understands customers better
It can only talk: it has no way to look up an order
The FAQ page it answers from is out of date

reveal.narration: Here's what happened, four hundred times over. A customer asks where her order is, and the question reaches the FAQ bot. The bot understands the question perfectly well; the model was never the problem. But look at the diagram: there is no line from the bot to the orders system. With no way to look anything up, the only thing it can produce is text, so out goes the same polite apology. A smarter model would only apologise more elegantly, and a newer FAQ page still wouldn't contain Ana's parcel.

steps.caption: Saturday, 10:12 PM. Ana types into the website chat: "Where is my order ORB-10482?"
Her question reaches the FAQ bot. It understands it perfectly: she wants her order's status.
That status lives in the orders system: shipped with ParcelPath, tracking PP-88213.
But there's no arrow from the bot to the orders system. No tool, no access, no way to ask.
So the bot does the only thing it can do: it writes text.
Reply sent: "I'm sorry, I can't access order information." Ana writes back, angrier.
Repeat 400 times over one weekend. The model was fine. It could talk, but it couldn't act.

hook.wrap_correct: Exactly. The model understood every question; it simply had no way to reach the orders system. With nothing to look up and nothing it could do, all it could produce was words. That missing piece, the ability to act through tools, is what turns a chatbot into an agent.
hook.wrap_wrong: Not quite. A bigger model would only write a more elegant apology, and a fresher FAQ page still wouldn't contain Ana's parcel. Look at the diagram: there's no line from the bot to the orders system. It could understand and talk, but it had no way to look anything up or act.
hook.wrap_point: An agent is a language model that can act: it decides which tools to use, uses them and works toward a goal, instead of only replying with text.

examples.title: The FAQ chatbot answers Ana
examples.intro: Orbit's chatbot gets a real customer question. Watch where its answer comes from, and where it can't come from.
examples.narration: Ana ordered a tent four days ago, and she wants to know where it is. She asks the website chat, which is Orbit's FAQ chatbot: a capable language model with the FAQ page pasted into its prompt. It understands her question perfectly. But the FAQ only knows general shipping times, and the chatbot has no connection to the orders system where her status lives. With nothing to look up, it does the only thing it can: it writes text. Ana gets a polite apology and the standard shipping times, and she is no closer to her tent.

predict.stem: Ana asks the FAQ chatbot: "Where is my order ORB-10482?" What will it reply?

options.text: A polite apology plus general shipping times, because it can't see orders
Her real status: shipped with ParcelPath, tracking PP-88213
Nothing useful, because the question is too hard for a chatbot to understand

predict.rationale: The chatbot understands the question fine. What it lacks is access: the order status lives in Orbit's orders system, and the chatbot has no connection to it. So it falls back on the only thing in its prompt, the FAQ.

steps.caption: Ana types into the website chat: "Hi, where is my order ORB-10482? It's been four days."
Her message reaches the FAQ chatbot: a capable language model with the FAQ page pasted into its prompt.
The FAQ says standard shipping takes 3 to 5 business days. It says nothing about Ana's order.
Ana's real status sits in the orders system. The chatbot has no connection to it and no way to ask.
Reply: "I'm sorry, I can't access order information. Standard shipping takes 3 to 5 business days."
Polite, instant and no help to Ana. A less careful bot might even guess "it's on its way!" with nothing behind it.

examples.title: Scout the agent answers Ana
examples.intro: Same customer, same question, but this time the model has one tool and decides for itself when to use it.
examples.narration: Now the same question goes to Scout, an agent. Scout runs on the same kind of language model, but it has a goal, to answer Ana with her real order status, and one tool: an order lookup called get_order. Scout reads the question and decides it needs facts it doesn't have. It asks for the lookup; your code runs it and hands back the result: shipped with ParcelPath, with a tracking number. Scout reads that, decides it now knows enough, and writes a reply with the real status. Perceive, decide, act, then look at the result: one trip round the agent loop.

predict.stem: Scout has one tool, get_order. What will it do first?

options.text: Call get_order with ORB-10482
Reply with the standard shipping times from the FAQ
Ask Ana to confirm her order number before doing anything

predict.rationale: The answer depends on facts Scout doesn't have, and Ana already gave her order number, so the lookup is the most useful next step. Asking again would waste her time; replying with shipping times would repeat the chatbot's mistake.

steps.caption: Same customer, same question, this time to Scout: "Hi, where is my order ORB-10482? It's been four days."
Scout reads it. Its goal: answer Ana with her real order status. It has one tool, get_order.
Scout decides it needs facts it doesn't have, and asks to call get_order with order_id ORB-10482.
Your code runs the lookup and returns: Trailhead 2P tent, shipped, ParcelPath, tracking PP-88213.
The result goes back to Scout. It decides it now has everything it needs: no second lookup.
Reply: "Your Trailhead 2P tent has shipped with ParcelPath. Your tracking number is PP-88213."
Same kind of model as the chatbot. The difference: a goal, a tool, and the freedom to decide when to use it.

examples.title: When no agent is needed: the shipping email
examples.intro: A job with fixed steps, and why a plain workflow beats an agent here.
examples.narration: Not every job at Orbit needs an agent. When Sam's warehouse marks an order as shipped, the customer should get an email with the tracking number. The steps never change: the orders system reports the change, a template fills in the name, the item and the tracking number, and the email goes out. There is nothing to decide, so there is no language model in this picture at all. It runs in about a second, costs almost nothing, and does exactly the same thing every time. And there's a bonus: customers who already have their tracking number are far less likely to ask where their order is.

predict.stem: Orbit wants every customer to get an email with their tracking number the moment their order ships. What should handle it?

options.text: A fixed workflow: the same three steps every time
Scout, so it can decide what to write to each customer
The FAQ chatbot, whenever a customer asks

predict.rationale: Nothing here needs deciding: the trigger, the content and the recipient are all known in advance. A workflow does it faster, cheaper and the same way every time. An agent would add cost and room for mistakes, and a chatbot only answers when asked.

steps.caption: Sam's warehouse marks ORB-10482 as shipped. The orders system announces the change.
A fixed template fills in Ana's name, the Trailhead 2P tent and tracking number PP-88213.
The email goes out to ana@example.com.
Done in about a second. No model call, no decisions, almost no cost, and the same result every time.
Bonus: with the tracking number already in her inbox, Ana may never need to ask where her order is.

guided.situation: Priya has found you a desk and a laptop. Before Scout can look up a single order, it needs a home: a project folder, Python and a working connection to the model. Today you set that up and build a small chatbot, so you can see for yourself what Orbit's FAQ bot can and can't do.

solved_case.label: Published solution walkthrough
solved_case.title: How a customer-service agent learned to look up and cancel orders
solved_case.source_label: Anthropic Claude Cookbooks — Customer Service Agent with Client-Side Tools
solved_case.source_note: This is an official, runnable reference implementation. It uses synthetic customer and order records so the complete solution can be studied safely.
solved_case.problem: A language model can write a helpful reply, but it cannot know a customer's record, retrieve an order status, or cancel an order unless the application gives it controlled access to those operations.
solved_case.solution: The published implementation gives Claude three client-side tools, executes the selected operation in application code, returns the tool result to Claude, and then asks Claude to produce the final customer-facing answer.
solved_case.result: The completed notebook successfully retrieves a customer's email, reports that order O2 is Processing, and confirms the cancellation of order O1. Each answer is grounded in the returned tool result.
evidence: Customer C1 is resolved through get_customer_info and the returned email is used in the final answer.
Order O2 is resolved through get_order_details and its Processing status is reported.
Order O1 is sent to cancel_order and the final response is written only after the tool returns success.

solution_steps.title: Describe the operations as tools
solution_steps.purpose: Make each business capability understandable and callable by the model.
solution_steps.explanation: The solution declares three tools: get_customer_info, get_order_details, and cancel_order. Each definition gives the operation a precise description and a JSON input schema, including the required customer_id or order_id.
solution_steps.code:
tools = [
  tool("get_customer_info", required="customer_id"),
  tool("get_order_details", required="order_id"),
  tool("cancel_order", required="order_id"),
]
solution_steps.result: Claude can now choose a named operation and supply a schema-valid identifier instead of inventing customer or order data.

solution_steps.title: Back each tool with application code
solution_steps.purpose: Keep data access and business actions inside deterministic code.
solution_steps.explanation: The reference implementation creates ordinary Python functions for customer lookup, order lookup, and cancellation. Its records are synthetic, but the same boundary can call a real CRM or order-management API without changing the model-facing tool contract.
solution_steps.result: Facts and state-changing actions come from controlled application functions rather than the model's memory.

solution_steps.title: Route the requested tool
solution_steps.purpose: Translate Claude's tool request into the correct application function.
solution_steps.explanation: A small dispatcher receives the requested tool name and its structured input. It calls only the matching function and passes the required identifier. This is the controlled bridge between model reasoning and business logic.
solution_steps.result: The model selects an allowed operation, while the application remains responsible for executing it.

solution_steps.title: Return tool evidence before asking for an answer
solution_steps.purpose: Ground the customer-facing response in the result of the real operation.
solution_steps.explanation: When the response stops for tool use, the application executes that request, appends Claude's tool request and the matching tool result to the message history, and calls the model again. The loop ends only when Claude returns a normal answer.
solution_steps.code:
while response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    call = next_tool_call(response)
    result = run_tool(call.name, call.input)
    messages += [response_message(response), tool_result(call.id, result)]
    response = ask_claude(messages, tools)
solution_steps.result: Claude receives evidence from the application before composing the response, so the final answer can cite the actual status or action result.

solution_steps.title: Verify the solved requests
solution_steps.purpose: Prove that the implementation performs the intended support jobs.
solution_steps.explanation: The notebook runs three completed requests: retrieve customer C1's email, report order O2's status, and cancel order O1. The printed trace shows the selected tool, its structured input, its returned value, and the final answer.
solution_steps.code:
ask("What is the status of order O2?")
ask("Please cancel order O1 for me.")
solution_steps.result: The final trace reports O2 as Processing and confirms that O1 was cancelled—demonstrating lookup, action, and evidence-grounded response generation.

steps.title: Make your first model call
steps.body: hello.py sends one message to the model and prints the reply. It's the smallest useful program in the course.
actions: Create **hello.py** in the **scout** folder and paste the code below.
Run it with `python hello.py`.

values.label: hello.py
values.value:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"

response = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL,
    max_tokens=16000,  # a ceiling, not a target
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "In one sentence, what is an AI agent?"}],
)

# The reply can contain several blocks (the model may think first), so take the text block:
text = next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
print(text)
print(f"Tokens used: {response.usage.input_tokens} in, {response.usage.output_tokens} out")

steps.check: After a few seconds you see a one-sentence answer, then a line with the token counts.
steps.tip: An error about authentication ("Could not resolve authentication method" or AuthenticationError) means the key isn't set in this terminal or is wrong: repeat step 4. "No module named 'anthropic'" means the environment isn't active: repeat step 2. A message about your credit balance means you need to add credit under **Billing**.

steps.title: Turn it into a chatbot that remembers
steps.body: A chatbot is a loop: read what you type, send the whole conversation to the model, print the reply, repeat. The messages list is its memory.
actions: Create **chat.py** in the **scout** folder and paste the code below.
Run it with `python chat.py`.
Type `Hi, I'm Ana.` and then ask `What's my name?`
Type `quit` to exit.

values.label: chat.py
values.value:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"
SYSTEM = (
    "You are Scout, Orbit Outdoor's support assistant. "
    "Orbit is an online shop for hiking, camping and climbing gear. "
    "Be friendly and brief."
)

messages = []  # the whole conversation so far: this list is Scout's memory

print("Scout is ready. Type quit to exit.")
while True:
    user_text = input("You: ").strip()
    if user_text.lower() == "quit":
        break
    if not user_text:
        continue

    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    response = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=16000,
        system=SYSTEM,
        messages=messages,
    )
    text = next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": text})
    print(f"Scout: {text}\n")

steps.check: Scout greets you, and when you ask your name it answers Ana. Typing quit ends the program.
steps.tip: If Scout forgets your name, check that both append lines are there: one for your message and one for Scout's reply. Without them, every call starts from zero, because the model itself remembers nothing between calls.

win.text: it remembered ana's name. you have no idea how many tickets start with "as i said in my last message..."

lab.title: Agent, chatbot or workflow?
lab.intro: Three requests landed in your inbox this week from Orbit's team. For each one, decide what kind of system it really needs, and remember that the most impressive option isn't always the right one.

scenarios.title: Sam's Monday stock report
scenarios.situation: Every Monday, Sam spends 40 minutes copying numbers from the stock sheet into an email for Maya and Leo: what's low, what's out, what's arriving. The sheet and the email look the same every week. Sam asks whether the new AI project could take this off his plate.

context.label: Sam's message
lines: sam: every monday i build the same stock report by hand
sam: same sheet, same columns, same two people
sam: anything under 2 in stock goes in a 'low' list
sam: could it just land in their inbox at 8 AM?

scenarios.stem: What should Orbit build for Sam?

options.text: A scheduled workflow: every Monday at 8, read the sheet, list low and out-of-stock items, email the report
options.why: Every step is known in advance and nothing needs judgement. A workflow does it the same way every week, in seconds, for almost nothing.

options.text: An agent that checks the stock sheet and decides when a report would be useful
options.why: Nothing here needs deciding, so an agent only adds cost, delay and the risk of a different report each week. Sam wants the same report, on time.

options.text: A chatbot that Sam, Maya and Leo can ask about stock levels
options.why: That might be handy later, but Sam asked for a report that arrives by itself. A chatbot waits to be asked.

hints: Could you write every step down before Monday comes?
If the steps never change, does anything need to decide them?
scenarios.debrief: When the trigger, the steps and the output are all known in advance, build a workflow. It's cheaper, faster and easier to trust than an agent. Experienced builders reach for an agent only when the steps depend on the request.

scenarios.title: Leo's customers, in their own words
scenarios.situation: Leo wants customers to get help at any hour, in their own words, without waiting for the team. Most messages are about orders, returns and exchanges, and no two look alike. Answering them means checking the order, the policy and sometimes the stock, in a different order each time. Every answer would be logged, so Leo can spot and fix mistakes.

context.label: This morning's queue (sample)
lines: #4472 Grace: can I still send back the boots from ORB-10517?
#4473 Owen: jacket's too big, can I swap the L for an M?
#4474 Ravi: my order says processing since tuesday, is that normal?

scenarios.stem: What kind of system fits Leo's request?

options.text: An agent: it reads each message, decides which lookups it needs (order, policy, stock) and answers from the results
options.why: The steps depend on the message, the answers need real lookups, and mistakes are recoverable. That's a textbook first agent job, and exactly what Scout is.

options.text: A bigger FAQ chatbot with every policy pasted into its prompt
options.why: It could explain the return policy, but it still can't see Grace's delivery date, the stock for Owen's swap or Ana's tracking number. It can talk, but not look anything up.

options.text: A workflow with one fixed branch for each type of question
options.why: Customers mix questions and phrase them in endless ways. Grace needs her order and the policy; Owen needs his order, the policy and the stock. Fixed branches multiply fast and still miss cases.

hints: Do all four messages need the same steps, in the same order?
Check it against the three signs of a good first agent job: repetitive, needs lookups, recoverable.
scenarios.debrief: This passes all three tests from lesson 1.3: it repeats hundreds of times, the answers live in Orbit's systems, and a wrong answer can be caught and corrected. That's why Scout exists. One detail shows why the lookups matter: Grace's boots were delivered 62 days ago, outside the 30-day return window, so a good agent must check and say no politely rather than promise a return.

scenarios.title: Maya's website questions
scenarios.situation: Maya looked at the website's contact form: a third of all messages ask the same few things. How long does shipping take? Is there express? How long do I have to return something? The answers are already in Orbit's policy and change maybe once a year. Maya wants these answered instantly, right on the website.

context.label: Top contact-form questions, last 30 days
lines: How long do I have to return things?   84
Do I pay for return shipping?          61

scenarios.stem: What should Orbit put on the website for these questions?

options.text: A clear FAQ page, or a simple chatbot that answers from the policy text
options.why: The answers are fixed and already written down. No lookups and no decisions: a FAQ page, or a chatbot grounded in the policy, answers instantly and costs little.

options.text: An agent with tools for shipping times and return windows
options.why: There's nothing to look up for each customer: the answers are the same for everyone. Tools and a decision loop add cost and moving parts for no gain.

options.text: A weekly workflow that emails every customer the shipping and returns policy
options.why: Customers ask at the moment they need the answer. A weekly email nobody asked for won't be there when the question comes up.

hints: Does the answer change from one customer to the next?
What's the simplest thing that would answer these instantly?
scenarios.debrief: Fixed answers to common questions don't need an agent. A good FAQ page, or a chatbot that answers from the policy, does the job cheaply. Save the agent for questions where the answer depends on this customer's order. In fact, Monday's FAQ bot was fine for exactly these questions; it only failed when asked about a specific order.

variants.title: Day 3 · What makes it an agent
variants.stem: Priya shows you two prototypes. A answers questions using the FAQ text in its prompt. B reads the question, decides to call get_order, reads the result and then replies. Which one is an agent?

options.text: B, because it decides on its own steps and takes actions toward a goal
A, because it answers in fluent, natural language
Both, because both use a language model

variants.rationale: Using a language model doesn't make something an agent, and neither do fluent replies. B decides what to do next, acts with a tool and uses the result: the perceive, decide, act loop.

variants.title: Day 10 · Agent or workflow?
variants.stem: Maya wants each day's orders copied from the shop into the accounting sheet every night at 11 PM. The columns never change. An intern proposes an agent "so it can work out what to copy". What do you recommend?

options.text: A scheduled workflow: the same steps every night, no model needed
The agent, because it can adapt if something changes
A chatbot the accountant can ask for each night's orders

variants.rationale: The steps are known in advance and identical every night. A workflow is cheaper, faster and predictable; an agent adds model costs and the chance of a different result each night. Many jobs don't need an agent.

variants.title: Day 30 · Which part is failing?
variants.stem: A test version of Scout answers Elena's first question about her climbing rope order perfectly. Then she writes "ok, and when will it arrive?" and Scout replies "Which order do you mean?" Which core part is failing?

options.text: Memory: the earlier messages aren't being sent with the new question
Tools: it needs a better tracking lookup
Planning: it should split the question into more steps

variants.rationale: Scout looked up the order fine the first time, so its tools work. It lost track of which order the chat was about, which means the conversation isn't being kept and sent with each call. In chat.py, that's the messages list.
